### Section 2: Statement of Need

In the Eastwood neighborhood, a child’s zip code still predicts whether they will learn to read on time. Today, only [28]% of Eastwood Elementary and [School B] third-graders read at or above grade level, leaving nearly three out of four students behind at the exact moment the curriculum shifts from "learning to read" to "reading to learn" [District Report Card, 2025]. 

**A Widening Local Literacy Gap**
While literacy rates across [County Name] have begun to rebound over the past three years, Eastwood’s youngest learners are falling further behind. According to [State Dept. of Education, 2025], third-grade reading proficiency in Eastwood sits [24] percentage points below the county average ([52]%) and [29] points below the state benchmark ([57]%). The gap begins early: [65]% of incoming kindergartners in the neighborhood enter school below readiness benchmarks in phonemic awareness and letter recognition [District Kindergarten Readiness Assessment, 2025]. Moreover, longitudinal district data shows that this deficit compounds by grade level—since [2022], the percentage of Eastwood fifth-graders scoring "far below proficient" has grown by [14]%, signaling that students who miss foundational K–2 literacy skills are not catching up through standard classroom instruction alone [Local School District Data, 2025].

**Systemic Barriers and Service Gaps**
Despite the dedication of local educators, Eastwood schools face acute resource constraints. Average K–5 class sizes at neighborhood schools have reached [28] students, and the district currently funds only [one] reading specialist per [450] students [School District Budget Report, 2025]. Classroom teachers simply cannot provide the high-dosage, individualized phonemic and comprehension instruction required to close multi-year reading gaps during the regular school day. 

Outside of school hours, affordable literacy intervention is virtually nonexistent in Eastwood. A [2025] community asset mapping by [Local United Way/Planning Council] identified zero other free or sliding-scale after-school programs within a [three]-mile radius that offer structured, evidence-based reading tutoring. Private tutoring in the area averages $[55]–$[75] per hour—an impossible expense for Eastwood families, where the median household income is $[34,000] and [78]% of students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch [U.S. Census ACS, 2024]. Consequently, demand for our program far outpaces our current capacity: we maintained an active waitlist of [45] students throughout the [2024–2025] school year, with an average wait time of [four] months for a tutoring slot.

**Community Voice**
Eastwood parents and teachers consistently name after-school reading support as their highest priority. In our [Fall 2025] family needs assessment (n=[110] parents), [88]% of respondents cited "help catching up in reading" as their child’s most urgent academic need, ranking it above math support, homework help, and enrichment activities. As one Eastwood second-grade parent shared: *"[Insert 1–2 sentence quote here, e.g., 'The teacher told me my son is a year behind in reading, and he cries every night over his books. I work two jobs and don't know how to teach phonics, and we can't afford a private tutor.']"*

**The Urgency of Early Intervention**
The window to reverse these trends is narrow and urgent. National longitudinal research confirms that children who are not reading proficiently by the end of third grade are four times more likely to leave high school without a diploma—a risk that rises to six times higher for children from low-income households [Annie E. Casey Foundation, *Double Jeopardy*]. In Eastwood, where high school graduation rates already lag the county by [15]% [State Ed Data, 2025], failing to intervene in the K–5 years locks students into a cycle of academic frustration, chronic absenteeism, and diminished economic mobility. 

To disrupt this trajectory and address the acute shortage of individualized literacy support in our community, our program focuses resources directly on the Eastwood K–5 students facing the steepest barriers to reading proficiency.

***

### Section 3: Target Population

**Volume and Geographic Focus**
Our program will serve 120 unduplicated K–5 students (ages 5–11) each year—[240] students total over the [two-year] grant period—who reside in the Eastwood neighborhood (zip codes [XXXXX] and [XXXXX]) or attend [Eastwood Elementary] and [School B]. 

**Eligibility Criteria and Verification**
To ensure our intensive tutoring slots reach the students with the highest academic and financial need, participants must meet two primary criteria:
1. **Academic Need:** Reading at least one half-year to two full years below grade level. We verify this prior to enrollment using school-provided benchmark assessments ([DIBELS / i-Ready / STAR Reading] scores) and direct teacher or school reading specialist referral forms. 
2. **Economic Need:** Household income at or below [185]% of the Federal Poverty Level. To minimize enrollment barriers for families, we verify this via student qualification for Free or Reduced-Price Lunch (FRPL) on school referral forms or a simplified parent income self-attestation at intake.

**Demographic Profile and Compounded Risk**
Reflecting our current program roster and neighborhood demographics, our target population is approximately [55]% [Hispanic/Latino], [30]% [Black/African American], [10]% [White], and [5]% [Multiracial/Other] [Internal Program Data, 2025]. Nearly [85]% of our students come from low-income households, and [40]% are English Learners (ELs) living in homes where a language other than English is primarily spoken. 

These students face intersecting systemic barriers that put them at the highest risk for long-term reading failure. Beyond attending under-resourced schools, [60]% of our families report living in single-parent households or working non-standard shift hours, limiting their bandwidth to navigate complex reading interventions at home [Internal Intake Data, 2025]. Furthermore, EL students in Eastwood face a dual challenge: acquiring foundational English phonics while simultaneously trying to keep pace with grade-level comprehension, often without bilingual literacy resources at home. Finally, transportation and safety concerns prevent many Eastwood parents from accessing enrichment programs outside the immediate neighborhood.

To meet these 120 students exactly where they are, we have designed a research-backed, accessible tutoring model that removes family barriers and accelerates literacy growth.

***

3. **Signed School Partnership MOU (Memorandum of Understanding):** An agreement with [Eastwood Elementary / District] confirming data-sharing permissions (so teachers can legally send you [DIBELS/i-Ready] scores) and direct student referral pathways.

### Section 4: Program Design & Activities

**Theory of Change & Logic Model Summary**
Our program operates on a clear theory of change: if K–5 students who are reading below grade level receive high-dosage, explicit, and systematic literacy instruction tailored to their specific skill deficits—and if structural barriers like cost, transportation, and language are removed—then students will accelerate their reading growth, close achievement gaps by third grade, and build the academic confidence needed for long-term school success. 

As detailed in our attached Logic Model, our **inputs** (certified reading specialists, trained tutors, evidence-based Science of Reading curricula, and school partnerships) drive two core **activities** (intensive 1:1 tutoring and small-group literacy labs). These yield immediate **outputs** (120 students receiving [48–60] hours of individualized instruction annually) that produce measurable short- and long-term **outcomes** (mastery of foundational phonics, at least [1.2] years of reading growth per school year, and grade-level reading proficiency).

**Core Activities & Links to Community Need**
Our instructional design directly addresses the overcrowded classrooms, specialist shortages, and dual-language barriers identified in Section 2 by delivering two tiered interventions at our neighborhood center and on-site at [Eastwood Elementary]:

1. **One-on-One Intensive Tutoring (Tier 3 Intervention):** Designed for our highest-need students ([60] students/year reading 1.5 to 2+ years behind, primarily struggling with K–2 foundational skills). Students meet with a dedicated tutor three times per week for 45-minute sessions across a 30-week academic year ([67.5] hours/year total dosage). Using the Orton-Gillingham-aligned [Wilson Fundations / UFLI Foundations] curriculum, sessions follow a structured literacy block: 10 minutes of phonemic awareness warm-ups, 20 minutes of explicit phonics and decoding, and 15 minutes of decodable text fluency. This 1:1 ratio provides the immediate corrective feedback and individualized pacing impossible in a 28-student classroom.
2. **Small-Group Literacy Labs (Tier 2 Intervention):** Designed for students reading 0.5 to 1.5 years behind ([60] students/year, focusing heavily on grades 3–5 transition and ELs). Grouped homogeneously by skill level in a strict 1:3 tutor-to-student ratio, cohorts meet twice weekly for 60-minute sessions ([60] hours/year dosage). Using [SIPPS / Reading Mastery], sessions combine explicit vocabulary and morphological instruction with guided comprehension strategies, directly addressing the third-grade shift from "learning to read" to "reading to learn."

**Evidence Base**
Our model is anchored in the Science of Reading and national best practices for high-dosage tutoring. Meta-analyses by the [Annenberg Institute at Brown University, 2023] and the [What Works Clearinghouse] confirm that tutoring delivered at least three times per week in groups of three or fewer during or immediately after school produces effect sizes equivalent to [3 to 5] additional months of learning. Furthermore, explicit, systematic phonics combined with oral language scaffolding is recognized by the [Institute of Education Sciences (IES)] as the gold-standard intervention for low-income students and English Learners acquiring literacy in a second language.

**Participant Pathway & Assessment Points**
Every student moves through a structured, data-driven pathway:
* **Referral & Intake (Weeks 1–3):** Teachers and families submit referrals; staff verify FRPL status and collect school-administered baseline [DIBELS 8th Edition / i-Ready] data.
* **Diagnostic & Cohort Assignment (Week 4):** Our Reading Specialist administers a 20-minute diagnostic phonics inventory to pinpoint exact skill gaps and assigns the student to a 1:1 tutor or 1:3 cohort.
* **Progress Monitoring (Ongoing & Mid-Year):** Tutors log daily session trackers and conduct bi-weekly 3-minute curriculum-based fluency probes. A formal mid-point assessment ([DIBELS/i-Ready]) in January informs cohort adjustments.
* **Exit & Follow-Up (May & November):** Students complete an exit benchmark in May. Those reaching grade level graduate to our light-touch homework club; others retain priority placement for fall. We track 6-month follow-up school reading scores the following November to verify sustained gains.

**Staffing, Caseloads, and Program Fidelity**
Tutors include paraprofessionals, pre-service education undergraduates from [Local University], and trained community members who complete [25] hours of pre-service Science of Reading training. Each part-time tutor manages a caseload of [6–8] students. To ensure instructional fidelity, our full-time, state-certified Lead Reading Specialist (1.0 FTE) supervises all tutors, conducts bi-weekly observations using a standardized fidelity rubric, and leads weekly 30-minute data huddles to review student progress dashboards.

**Accessibility Supports**
To eliminate participation barriers for Eastwood families, we provide: (1) safe "walking school buses" from [Eastwood Elementary] and [School B] directly to our center; (2) bilingual ([Spanish/English]) tutors, family liaisons, and translated progress reports; (3) healthy daily after-school snacks; and (4) flexible late-pickup windows (until [6:30 PM]) plus a live virtual tutoring option via [Zoom] for students facing sudden family illness or shift-work scheduling conflicts.

**Key Deliverables & Quarterly Milestones**
* **Q1 (Jul–Sep):** Finalize school MOUs; recruit/train [18] tutors; enroll 120 students and complete baseline diagnostics.
* **Q2 (Oct–Dec):** Deliver [1,400]+ tutoring hours; conduct bi-weekly fidelity checks; host Fall Family Literacy Night.
* **Q3 (Jan–Mar):** Complete mid-year assessments; re-level cohorts; hold mid-year teacher/parent conferences.
* **Q4 (Apr–Jun):** Complete 30-week instructional cycle ([7,500]+ total student hours); run exit assessments and annual evaluation.

**Risks & Mitigations**
To mitigate **attendance drops**, we tie attendance to a student book-reward incentive system and deploy bilingual staff to call families after two consecutive absences. To mitigate **tutor turnover**, we offer paid stipends and course-credit partnerships with [Local University]. To prevent **data-sharing delays**, signed parental FERPA releases are collected at intake so we can pull scores directly from parents and teachers.

### Section 6: Outcomes & Objectives (~395 words)

To ensure our program translates instructional hours into lasting academic gains for Eastwood’s K–5 students, we separate service delivery metrics (**Outputs**) from measurable changes in student literacy (**Outcomes**). 

**Annual Program Outputs**
* **Enrollment & Dosage:** Serve 120 unduplicated K–5 students annually ([60] in 1:1 Tier 3 tutoring; [60] in 1:3 Tier 2 labs), delivering at least [7,500] total tutoring hours across the 30-week school year.
* **Attendance & Retention:** Maintain an average student attendance rate of [85]% or higher across all scheduled sessions and a full-year program retention rate of at least [88]% (up from a historical neighborhood after-school baseline of [70]%).

**SMART Program Outcomes**
Our objectives are anchored in baseline data from our [2024–2025] cohort, where [0]% of incoming students read at grade level at intake and the average baseline reading deficit was [1.4] years behind grade level:

1. **Objective 1: Foundational Phonics Mastery (Short-Term Outcome):** By May of each grant year, **85% of K–2 and Tier 3 participants** (102+ students) will master at least [80]% of targeted grade-level phonemic awareness and decoding skills, up from a baseline average of [32]% mastery at intake, as measured by the [Wilson Fundations / UFLI] Diagnostic Phonics Inventory and bi-weekly curriculum-based mastery probes.
2. **Objective 2: Accelerated Reading Growth (Intermediate Outcome):** By May of each grant year, **80% of all enrolled K–5 students** (96+ students) will achieve at least **1.3 years of reading growth** within a single 30-week academic year—exceeding the standard 1.0-year benchmark required to begin closing multi-year achievement gaps—as measured by pre-, mid-, and post-test scale scores on school-administered [i-Ready Diagnostic / STAR Reading] assessments.
3. **Objective 3: Grade-Level Reading Benchmark & Oral Fluency (Long-Term Outcome):** By the conclusion of the grant period, **65% of students completing at least 50 hours of tutoring** will move up at least one proficiency tier (e.g., from "Well Below Benchmark" to "Approaching" or "At/Above Benchmark") on the [DIBELS 8th Edition] composite score, up from a baseline of [18]% among non-tutored peers with similar starting deficits. Additionally, **75% of graduating participants** will maintain or exceed their spring reading gains on their 6-month follow-up school benchmark the following November.

| Outcome Metric | Baseline (Intake) | Target (Exit) | Measurement Tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phonics/Decoding Mastery | 32% skill mastery | 85% reach ≥80% mastery | Diagnostic Phonics Inventory |
| Annual Reading Growth | <0.7 years/year | 80% achieve ≥1.3 years | School [i-Ready / STAR] Scale Score |
| Tier Advancement / Fluency | 0% at grade level | 65% advance ≥1 tier | [DIBELS 8th Ed.] Composite |

***

### Section 7: Evaluation Plan (~405 words)

**Evaluation Design & Methodology**
We utilize a rigorous pre-/mid-/post-test longitudinal evaluation design, supplemented by a quasi-experimental matched comparison analysis. Through our data-sharing MOU with [Eastwood Elementary / School District], we compare the reading growth of our 120 participants against an anonymized comparison group of [Eastwood] K–5 peers with similar baseline [DIBELS/i-Ready] scores and FRPL/EL demographics who did not participate in tutoring.

**Data Collection Tools, Frequency, and Responsibilities**
* **Standardized School Benchmarks (Baseline, Mid-Point, Exit, 6-Month Follow-Up):** Our Program Coordinator collects official [DIBELS 8th Edition] and [i-Ready] reports directly from school reading specialists in September (baseline), January (mid-point), May (exit), and the following November (sustained impact).
* **Diagnostic & Formative Curriculum Probes (Intake & Bi-Weekly):** Our certified Lead Reading Specialist administers the Diagnostic Phonics Inventory at intake (Week 4). Tutors administer 3-minute curriculum-based oral reading fluency (ORF) and decoding probes every two weeks, entering scores into our cloud-based data system ([Apricot / Salesforce]) within 24 hours of each session.
* **Qualitative & Fidelity Metrics (Monthly & Bi-Annually):** The Lead Reading Specialist conducts bi-weekly tutor observations using a standardized fidelity rubric. Bilingual staff administer parent and teacher satisfaction surveys in January and May.

**Data Quality, Privacy, and Security Procedures**
To ensure data accuracy, the Lead Reading Specialist audits [15]% of tutor-entered fluency probes monthly and conducts inter-rater reliability checks during pre-service training. All student records are protected in strict compliance with FERPA. Signed parental FERPA consent forms are collected at intake. Identifiable student data is stored on encrypted, password-protected servers with role-based access, and all reports shared with funders or external stakeholders use aggregated or de-identified student IDs.

**Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) & Reporting**
Evaluation is embedded into our weekly operations. Every Friday, the Lead Reading Specialist and tutors hold 30-minute data huddles to review real-time student dashboards. If a student’s bi-weekly probe shows flat growth for four consecutive weeks, the Specialist immediately modifies their instructional plan or shifts them from a 1:3 group to 1:1 tutoring. In January, mid-year [i-Ready/DIBELS] data is used to re-level cohorts and update classroom teachers. Comprehensive evaluation reports detailing progress toward all SMART objectives are shared with our Board of Directors quarterly and submitted to funders, partner principals, and Eastwood families at the end of each school year.

**Evaluation Timeline**
* **Q1 (Sep):** Collect FERPA releases; pull school baseline scores; run intake diagnostics.
* **Q2 (Oct–Dec):** Bi-weekly fluency probes; monthly fidelity audits; Q2 CQI data review.
* **Q3 (Jan–Feb):** Pull mid-year school benchmarks; re-level student cohorts; mid-year parent survey.
* **Q4 (May–Jun):** Administer exit diagnostics; pull spring school benchmarks; analyze annual growth vs. comparison group; publish Annual Impact Report (6-month follow-up data pulled in Nov).
